text: Frederick William MacMonnies (September 28, 1863 – March 22, 1937) was the most renowned expatriate American sculptor of the Beaux-Arts school, achieving equal acclaim in France and the United States. He was also a skilled painter and portraitist, born in Brooklyn Heights, Brooklyn, New York, and died in New York City. Among his best-known sculptures are Nathan Hale, Bacchante and Infant Faun, and Diana. In 1880, he began an apprenticeship under Augustus Saint-Gaudens, becoming a studio assistant and forming a lifelong friendship with him; in Saint-Gaudens' studio, he met Stanford White, who later sought his sculptural expertise for architectural projects. In 1884, MacMonnies traveled to Paris to study at the École des Beaux-Arts, winning the highest award twice as a foreign student. In 1888, he opened a studio in Paris and submitted works annually to the Paris Salon, mentoring artists such as Janet Scudder and Mary Foote; he also studied at the Académie Vitti in 1904. The 8-foot Nathan Hale statue, his first major commission, was erected in 1893 in New York City near where Nathan Hale is believed to have been executed; copies are held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art, Princeton University Art Museum, National Gallery of Art, Phoenix Art Museum, Orlando Museum of Art, and Mead Art Museum at Amherst College. In 1888, Stanford White secured two major commissions for MacMonnies: a Pan fountain for Edward Adams’s Rohallion mansion in New Jersey and a sculpture for ambassador Joseph H. Choate at Naumkeag in Stockbridge, Massachusetts. In 1889, an Honorable Mention at the Paris Salon for his Diana led to additional American commissions, including spandrel reliefs for Stanford White’s Washington Arch and the Nathan Hale memorial in City Hall Park, dedicated in 1893. Until World War I, MacMonnies traveled annually between the United States and Paris, returning to Paris to work on commissions, with his long-term residence at Giverny. In 1891, he designed the statue of James S. T. Stranahan in Brooklyn and was awarded the commission for the Columbian Fountain at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago, where the sculpture of Columbia in her Grand Barge of State became the iconic centerpiece of the American Beaux-Arts movement. In 1894, Stanford White commissioned three bronze groups for the Soldiers and Sailors Memorial Arch in Brooklyn’s Grand Army Plaza, a project that occupied MacMonnies for eight years. Around the turn of the century, he designed the equestrian statue of Henry Warner Slocum in Brooklyn, dedicated in 1905. Due to his fame from the 1893 Exposition, MacMonnies created a public sculpture celebrating American Old West pioneers, his only work on this subject, beginning in 1906 and unveiled in 1911; it depicts Kit Carson and marks the end of the Smoky Hill Trail near the Smoky Hill River. In 1904, his full-length painting of student Mabel Conkling was considered his "finest" painting to date. Commissioned in 1908, the Princeton Battle Monument, created with architects Carrere & Hastings, was not completed until 1922. After returning to New York in 1915, he created the colossal group Civic Virtue, a fountain for New York City Hall (1909–1922), which sparked public controversy due to its depiction of a man trampling female figures representing evil sirens; the statue was moved to Queens Borough Hall in 1941 and later to Green-Wood Cemetery in Brooklyn in December 2013. In late 1917, MacMonnies was commissioned by New York City citizens to create a sculpture in honor of those who died in the First Battle of the Marne, gifted to the French people in exchange for the Statue of Liberty; the resulting work, La Liberté éplorée ("The Tearful Liberty"), located in Meaux, France, is 22 meters (72 feet) tall and was completed in 1932, becoming the world’s largest stone monument at the time; the architect was Thomas Hastings. In 2011, the Musée de la Grande Guerre du pays de Meaux opened adjacent to the monument. A 9-foot (2.7-meter) bronze version of the statue is housed in the World War I Memorial in Atlantic City, New Jersey. In 1931, MacMonnies was selected to sculpt the fourth issue of the Society of Medalists, celebrating Charles Lindbergh’s 1927 solo trans-Atlantic flight with a powerful bust on the obverse and an allegorical eagle battling across the sea on the reverse, making it one of the series’ most popular issues. MacMonnies died of pneumonia in 1937 at age 73. He received the first Gold Medal ever awarded to an American sculptor at the Paris Salon and was elected Chevalier of the French Légion d’honneur in 1896; he also won the grand prize at the 1900 Paris Exposition. In 1901, he received an honorable mention at the Paris Salon for his first painting, and was selected to sculpt the Major General George B. McClellan statue, first exhibited at the 1906 Paris Salon. He was an early member of the American Academy of Arts and Letters and won a silver medal in the art competition at the 1932 Summer Olympics. In 1888, MacMonnies married Mary Louise Fairchild, who was studying in Paris on a three-year scholarship; upon marriage, the scholarship was voided, and they lived and worked in Paris, frequently returning to the United States. They shared prominence at the 1893 Chicago Exposition, with MacMonnies creating the Columbian Fountain and Mary painting the mural Primitive Woman for the Woman’s Building, with Mary Cassatt creating the facing work Modern Woman. As their fortunes grew, they bought a home in Giverny, the artists’ colony founded by Claude Monet, where they had three children: Berthe (1895), Marjorie (1897), and Ronald (1899). Their lives diverged as MacMonnies spent increasing time in Paris on large projects and maintained a long-term affair with Alice Jones, daughter of Nevada Senator and Santa Monica co-founder John P. Jones, with whom she bore a son. MacMonnies filed for divorce from Mary in 1909 (they had three children, two of whom survived infancy), and married Jones in 1910. During MacMonnies’s absences, Will Low, who spent summers in Giverny, developed an interest in Mary; when Low’s wife died nearly simultaneously with MacMonnies’s divorce, Mary and Low were married in 1909. They and Mary’s two daughters (Ronald died of meningitis in 1901) moved back to the United States in early 1910, while MacMonnies remained in Giverny. MacMonnies permanently relocated to the United States in 1915 due to the outbreak of World War I and lived in New York City until his death in 1937. He is interred in Ferncliff Cemetery, Hartsdale, Westchester County, New York, with an unmarked grave.
